text:
In the Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (Saffire-II), test 2-7 evaluated a PMMA-plus-Nomex composite sample [PSI-99:test2-7]. **The main outcome was that the Nomex material failed to ignite despite ignition of the PMMA pilot flame** [S-034 p.row 14], [S-041 p.web: last slide].

### Experimental Test Conditions
Pursuant to reporting requirements for microgravity combustion findings, the specific experimental conditions for this sample were:
* **Fuel Material:** PMMA & Nomex composite (utilizing PMMA hot-wire ignition) [S-020 p.4], [PSI-99:test2-7].
* **Sample Geometry:** Flat strip measuring 50 mm × 290 mm, with a thickness of 0.85 mm PMMA + 0.37 mm Nomex [S-034 p.row 10].
* **Oxygen Concentration:** $O_2$ mole fraction of 0.221 (22.1% $O_2$) [PSI-99:test2-7].
* **Forced Flow Velocity:** 20.0 cm/s [PSI-99:test2-7].
* **Ambient Pressure:** Unspecified (no numeric total pressure is recorded in the dataset) [S-062 p.web: p.6].
* **Hardware & Facility:** Saffire flow unit sample card inside the Cygnus cargo resupply vehicle after unberthing from the International Space Station [S-020 p.4], [S-062 p.web: p.6].

### Notice on Data Status & Gaps
* **Golden Table Status:** The summary record for Saffire-II in the table repository is designated as an **unverified LLM draft** [S-034 p.row 14].
* **Data Gaps:** The exact numeric total cabin pressure during the test run remains unknown/unspecified in the repository [S-062 p.web: p.6].

bundle.question: In Saffire-II, what happened to the PMMA-plus-Nomex composite sample?

facts.claim: To prevent decompression sickness ('the bends'), astronauts perform a pre-breathe protocol by inhaling 100% oxygen to purge dissolved nitrogen from body tissues.

To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.

In free fall, buoyancy-driven natural convection and buoyant rise of hot exhaust gases are absent, causing flames to behave dramatically differently from terrestrial flames; for example, a candle flame becomes a dim blue, spherical diffusion flame.

fields.flow_note: the PSI-99 CSV gives 20 cm/s for 2-6; the pre-flight plan gives 30 cm/s for S6/S9 — 20-25 chosen

fields.lunar_note: O2 upper bound and/or pressure lower bound unknown
fields.main_finding: None of the four silicone samples burned significantly in microgravity, and the source states that silicone flammability in microgravity appears reduced compared with 1-g at the flows tested; the 5 cm SIBAL strips burned completely (2.1 mm/s at 20 cm/s, 2.6 mm/s at 25 cm/s), while Nomex did not ignite despite the PMMA pilot flame.

experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains
structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The

On the morning of
day 2, the Mission Support Team should have the initial images to review. Operations for days 2-8 will consist of
identifying the specific raw images (i.e., uncompressed) to be downlinked, preparing the commands to downlink this
data, and preparing and issuing commands to downlink data packets that were requested but not received. Of course,
the raw images have a higher resolution that the compressed images and will be used for the majority of the science
analysis. By contract, Cygnus will remain in orbit for up to 8 days to downlink data or until 20 Gbits (2.5 Gbytes) of
data are received. When data downlink is completed, the relays that power the Saffire avionics will be opened,
officially ending the Saffire-I experiment. Following the experiment, detailed analysis of the results will commence by researchers at NASA GRC and the
“Fire Safety in Space” International Topical Team that has assisted in defining the Saffire experiments. Based on the
the current schedule, Saffire-II will be integrated into the OA-5 Cygnus PCM on May 12, 2016. The Saffire-II
launch is planned for no earlier than July 6 with operations occurring in September 2016. International Conference on Environmental Systems

[Saffire-II | S-020: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire) | B. Diagnostics]
This material will be expected to burn at the anticipated oxygen mole fraction of the
cabin atmosphere (near 0.21 O mole fraction). A second redundant igniter is woven into the fabric at the downstream end of the sample in case of a failure of the upstream igniter or if the flame does not propagate the
entire length of the sample. The objective of the tests to be conducted on Saffire-II is to investigate the low-gravity
Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) flammability limits in long-term low gravity.2 The configuration for these
experiments consists of nine samples of varying materials (denoted flammability samples) each having dimensions
of approximately 5 cm wide by 29 cm long installed on the same panel in place of the single sample in Fig. 1. The
Saffire-II sample card is shown in Fig. 2b. These samples emulate the configuration used in NASA-STD-6001 Test
1.3 Each sample is ignited at the bottom using a hot wire. The oxygen concentration in the Cygnus vehicle will be
nearly 21% by volume—the same as in the ISS when the hatch was closed. The materials have been selected to be
near their normal-gravity or hypothesized low-gravity maximum oxygen concentration in 21% O . This has complicated the selection of sample materials because most materials relevant for spacecraft do not have normal-gravity flammability limits near 21% oxygen by volume.4-6 Camera images are the primary diagnostics for these
tests as the intended result is primarily to determine whether the flame propagates or self-extinguishes.

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
